description_block:
It started as a black figural structure. I attempted to make a crucified figure. At the start it was a kind of cubic stretch-figure. But it wasnât successful. It was a stylistic platitude. So, I went on painting and the figure of Christ became a cross. And finally, this cross became veiled by a dark cloud. But I am quite satisfied that something is still perceptible. It doesnât even have to be consciously perceptible. He [Christ] withdraws when we attempt to represent him. Perhaps he is there in an intimation, in an extinguished, fragmentary way. In certain signs. And yet he even withdraws there. As soon as one thoughtlessly repeats it.(Arnulf Rainer, quoted in P. Friedhelm Mennekes, Rainer Michael Mason, Arnulf Rainer: Arnulf Rainer. Cross 1956-2009, NÃ¼rnberg, 2010, p. 27).   
Executed in 1982, Kreuz (Cross) belongs to one of the most significant and enduring motifs within Arnulf Rainer's oeuvre. Since the mid-1950s, the artist repeatedly returned to the image of the cross, employing it not only as a symbol rooted in Christian tradition but also as a means of exploring the limits of representation itself. As Rainer described, his crosses emerged from attempts to depict the figure of Christ, only to become increasingly obscured through the process of painting. The motif thus occupies a space between revelation and concealment, presence and absence.
The present work exemplifies Rainer's engagement with materiality and surface. Executed in oil on paper laid down on board, the work derives its visual strength from the interplay between its elements. The layered construction reinforces the vertical and horizontal axes of the composition, lending the cruciform structure a physical presence. Across this framework, Rainer applies dense passages of black pigment in vigorous gestures, activating the surface while preserving the clarity of the motif. Traces of the artist's intervention remain visible throughout, imbuing the work with a sense of energy and immediacy.
Situated within Rainer's celebrated body of Kreuz paintings and related Ãbermalungen (Overpaintings), the present work reflects the artist's sustained engagement with the motif of the Cross and its relationship to the figure of Christ. Rather than abandoning figuration altogether, Rainer subjects the image to a process of transformation, shifting the emphasis from representation to the physical act of painting itself. The cross remains legible, its structural presence reinforced by the layered support, while the expressive application of paint introduces movement, tension and ambiguity. Through this interplay of image, material and gesture, the work achieves both a powerful spiritual resonance and the striking material presence that characterises the artist's most accomplished works.
Widely regarded as one of the most important European artists of the post-war era, Arnulf Rainer developed a highly individual visual language in which religious imagery, gestural abstraction and the physical act of painting converge. His international importance has been affirmed through major retrospectives at the Centre Georges Pompidou, Paris, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York, and the Stedelijk Museum, Amsterdam. In the present work, these concerns coalesce with particular clarity, making Kreuz a compelling example of the artist's enduring engagement with the themes of revelation, concealment and transcendence.

description_block:
A rocky escarpment rises above a bend in the river, its surface articulated through bands of red, pink, violet, blue and white. Painted in 1942, SkÃ¡la a Åeka (Rock and River) belongs to the final years of VÃ¡clav Å pÃ¡la's career, when the artist had fully absorbed the lessons of Fauvism and Cubism into a highly personal approach to landscape painting.
The composition is dominated by the cliff that occupies much of the picture plane. Rather than describing the formation naturalistically, Å pÃ¡la constructs it through broad, angular brushstrokes that divide the rock face into interlocking planes of colour. Coral reds, pale pinks, blues and whites animate the surface, allowing colour to assume a structural role within the composition. The ascending diagonal of the cliff imparts a sense of movement, while the visible brushwork reinforces the immediacy of the artist's engagement with the subject. Below, the river provides a counterpoint to the solidity of the rock. Its calm surface reflects fragments of the landscape, echoing the colours of the escarpment across the lower edge of the canvas. Small figures along the riverbank establish a sense of scale, emphasising the imposing presence of the cliff, while a broad expanse of sky balances the density of the landform beneath.
Landscape occupied an increasingly important place within Å pÃ¡la's work from the 1920s onwards. The regions surrounding the Berounka and Otava rivers, which recur throughout his oeuvre, provided motifs through which he could continue to explore questions of colour, structure and form. In SkÃ¡la a Åeka, observation remains the point of departure, yet natural forms are reorganised through the artist's distinctive visual language. The influence of Cubism remains evident in the construction of the composition, while the intensity of the palette reflects Å pÃ¡la's longstanding commitment to colour as an expressive force.
As a founding member of both the Group of Fine Artists and later TvrdoÅ¡Ã­jnÃ­ (The Stubborn Ones), Å pÃ¡la played a central role in the development of Czech modernism. SkÃ¡la a Åeka reflects the mature synthesis of these achievements. The commanding cliff face, built from interlocking planes of colour, demonstrates the extent to which the artist had absorbed and transformed the lessons of Fauvism and Cubism into a language entirely his own. Combining structural clarity with painterly freedom, the present work ranks among the most accomplished paintings of Å pÃ¡la's mature years and stands as a particularly powerful expression of the artistic vision that defines his oeuvre.

description_block:
Conceived as both a linguistic exercise and an homage to the celebrated word-based works of Alighiero Boetti, 1111 originates from the phrase mettere i verbi all'infinito (or a variation thereof). Working against the clock, the artist allotted himself eleven minutes to identify as many four-letter English words as could be extracted from the Italian text. This process yielded eighty-three distinct words, each subsequently rendered as a colour print on canvas in a visual language evocative of Boetti's own practice.
The edition comprises twenty-one colour prints on canvas and a wooden support element, around which one of the canvases may be wrapped for display. Presented in groups of four, the words form a series of four-word compositions that oscillate between the poetic and the enigmatic, inviting the viewer to navigate shifting relationships between language, chance and meaning. Through its playful yet systematic methodology, 1111 reflects the artist's enduring engagement with permutation, authorship and the transformative potential of text.
material: colour print on canvas, wooden support element
provenance: Private Collection, Italy
subject_matter: four-letter words, color prints, canvas, typography, geometric patterns, abstract forms, compositions, linguistic exercise, visual language, homage

description_block:
Powerful large-scale piece from a key figure of Viennese ActionismHighly expressive and physical mixed-media work, combining painting with performanceStriking use of black pigment adds visual drama and underscores Nitschâs emotionally charged late work

Created in 2005, this large-scale mixed media work exemplifies the visceral and ritualistic nature of Hermann Nitschâs practice, closely aligned with the principles of his Orgien-Mysterien-Theater (Theatre of Orgies and Mysteries). The artist is a central figure of Viennese Actionism, sought to evoke emotional catharsis through the synthesis of painting, performance, and spiritual symbolism.
Applied with pronounced physicality, the workâs gestural fields of colour on a dual support consisting of paper mounted on wood recall both the immediacy of Action Painting and the structured intensity of ritual procedure. The concentrated use of black pigment plays a central visual and compositional role. As Nitsch once remarked, âI like black a lot. There are many painters who say that âblack is the king of color.â (Hermann Nitsch citied in: Paul Laster, âI Think Art Is a Way of Intensity. Interview with Hermann Nitsch,â Interview, Artpulse Magazine, 2015, online.)
Rather than serving purely as contrast, the black functions as a zone of formal compression. It simultaneously draws in and obstructs the viewerâs gaze, appearing both absorptive and impenetrable. This tension between attraction and resistance establishes a visual intensity that defines the workâs surface.
The work does not depict a traditional subject. Instead, it documents a process, presenting the residue of an event shaped by performative gesture and material encounter. In this sense, the painting functions as a site of accumulation rather than representation and offers a direct record of Nitschâs ongoing engagement with painting as action.
